However, McCall and Dunn argue that "local spatial knowledge is often more reliable than scientific knowledge 'because it embodies generations of practical essential knowledge, and it operates in interactive, holistic systems'" (McCall andDunn, 2012 quoting McCall andMianng, 2005).

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The Participatory GIS process is completed through a variety of methods. In many cases, PGIS is completed through a participatory PRA process and transferred to the maps. The layering capabilities of GIS allow multiple voices and perspectives to be viewed simultaneously. Soft GIS methodology creates a connection through the use of "affordances," which are the "perceived opportunities and restrictions concerning a person's actions in a given environment… [It] is not a characteristic of the environment, or a characteristic of the individual, but rather it is something between them." (Kahila and Kyttӓ, 2010;Ratanen and Kahila, 2009). Similarly, Talen explains that questions such as: 'Where are the roads most congested?' becomes 'What streets do I view as undesirable owing to traffic congestion?" (Talen, 1999). This concept of "affordances" allows researchers and decision makers to consider resident perceptions, or local knowledge, in their Adapted from: https://www.geospatialworld.net/article/should-pgis-serve-two-masters/ analysis; whereas, typical neighborhood research relies on standard indicators for socioeconomic data (Talen, 1999, citing others).

There are many suggestions in the literature for creating a successful GIS project:  Quality of data is inextricably linked to sampling design and participation rates (Brown and Kyttӓ, 2014)  Careful consideration of inclusion in every stage (McCall and Dunn, 2012) o "Participation cuts across the process from gaining a clear understanding of the existing legal and regulatory frameworks, to jointly setting project objectives, defining strategies and choosing appropriate geo-spatial information management tools" (Rambaldi, Kwaku Kyem, McCall, and Weiner, 2006) o "Flow of information between different actors is critical" (Kahila and Kyttӓ, 2010)  Respect the integrity of local knowledge (McCall and Dunn, 2012)  Choosing a scale for the information that meets demands for "coverage, comprehensiveness and inclusion on one hand, and on the other hand, information digestion (rather than overload), simplicity and comprehension" (McCall and Dunn, 2012)  The ability to locate affordances on a map (Brown and Kyttӓ, 2012;Talen, 1999)  "Feasibility, local manageability, technical sustainability, and currency, resulting also in cost-effectiveness" (McCall and Dunn, 2012)  Customization (Brown and Kyttӓ, 2012)  Good governance -"accountability, legitimacy, transparency, responsiveness, participation, respect for rights, equity, local usability, and other dimensions" (Rambaldi, Kwaku Kyem, McCall, and Weiner, 2006citing McCall 2003and McCall et al. 2005)  Willingness of decision-makers to use the knowledge and methods in their work (Ratanen andKahila, 2009, Brown andKyttӓ, 2012) Although PGIS has been used around the world for various projects, the literature and studies remain quite sparse. Most of the examples of PGIS are done by NGOs and community groups, and are not recorded or published. Brown and Kyttӓ report that "there have only been two longitudinal PGIS studies (Brown & Donovan, 1013b;Brown & Weber, 2011) and one meta-study using PPGIS data (Brown, 2013a)" (Brown and Kyttӓ, 2012).

PGIS is often seen as an element of decision-support rather than a tool for decision analysis (Greene, Devillers, Luther, and Eddy, 2011) PGIS users can reinforce empowerment through the exploratory function of GIS-based decision tools (McCall, 2003citing Carver 2001), and these tools will aid in fulfilling the bottom-up planning, democratic empowerment, and advocacy (McCall, 2003citing Weiner & Harris, 2002and Gonzalez, 2000;Brown and Kyttӓ, 2012;Rantanen and Kahila, 2009). Brown and Kyttӓ state that "the potential of PPGIS as a foundation for iterative public participation, rather than a singular by-product of a public participation process, appears large. Future research could explore the use of PPGIS throughout a complete planning cycle, from scoping to alternative development to decision and monitoring" (Brown and Kyttӓ, 2012).
